reading_text: Something green has taken hold in the thin soil at the foot of the scree, small and new and quietly rooted. The meltwater finds its own way down through the stones, never asking which channel, only following the pull of the slope. Under the loose rock lies the old bedrock, the ground your footing has always come from, whether or not you saw it. It was the storms of many springs that broke the mountain down to this — each stone that fell paid for the slope you now stand on. And still the scree holds, unmoved by the wind that has thrown itself against it for a hundred years, settled deeper with every assault. What has been quietly holding you up while you looked elsewhere for the ground?

One voice lifts the first line of the song alone, into a quiet that has not yet decided what to hold, and the note hangs there unwritten. Then a second voice finds it, low and sure, the way water finds the lowest curve of the ground and settles. The tune moves through the room at its own pace, line by line, no one hurrying it, each breath falling where the one before it left off. The warmth that started the song is an old one, carried from rooms you have already sat in, and it still steadies the throat now. There is one line ahead that not every voice will reach, the verse that catches in the chest before it opens, and the room slows where it comes. When the song thins to that one held note, whose voice do you hear still carrying it?

The keys to the old house still lie in your palm, warm from your own hand, though another turns the lock at night now. This is what passes between people who share a roof, the giving and the taking that keeps a household level. Something in that closed house is still growing quietly, the way a garden goes on setting fruit whether or not anyone comes to gather it. Under all of it sits the plain fact of walls that were once yours and are now only remembered, a home that stays a home in you even as the door answers to someone else. What brought you here was never fully in view, the small turns and chances that decided who stayed and who went, hidden the way a stair worn smooth hides the years of feet that wore it. Holding those keys asks something honest of you, a reckoning of what was fairly given and what was quietly kept back. If nothing shifts, the metal stays in your grip and the lock stays another's, and both of you go on living beside a door neither will open.

The road runs beside the river here, close to the water where the bank holds firm, and where you walk it the ground does not give way beneath you. It winds past the old turf houses your people left standing, and the road does not stop for them, it carries their shape forward as it goes. Underfoot the track keeps the pace the land gives it, faster where the ground falls, slower on the climb, never hurried and never still. The river has been speaking the whole way, a low sound at your side that told you where the ground was sound long before your feet did. Ahead the road bends with the water and slips out of sight around the next rise, going where the river goes, keeping its company. What lies past the bend is not yours to see from here, and the walking is enough.

The line runs down into dark water and nothing has touched it yet, and something waits under the surface that has not shown itself. Light comes slow across still water, and what was one grey sheet becomes water and sky, two things where there was one. The pull that runs down that thin line into the deep is stronger than it looks, old and unhurried, the kind of strength that mends by taking its own time. Behind you the water gives no reflection and keeps what it holds, and you cannot read it however long you look. If the line stays down and you stay with it, what rises will be yours to know, felt hand to hand along the taut length of it. The water is calm and you are holding it steady.

The old farmstead stands roofless now, and yet the walls still speak, stone answering stone in a language older than the family who raised them. Beyond the fallen gable the field opens grey and unbroken, nothing sown there yet, nothing owed. The doorway still stands, its lintel low, and the single thorn of a wild rose has grown across the threshold where the door once hung. This ground has taken in many harvests and given them all back, working slow through frost and thaw long before any hand came to gather. The hearthstone holds warmth in memory alone, and the walls keep the shape of a home no one lives in now. What was built here is not what stands here, and the field beyond the wall does not remember the house at all.

The flock stands quiet in the field at dusk, Anna, not yet turned toward the fold, waiting on something in the light before it moves. When they go they go together, warm bodies drifting one after another through the open gate, the whole of it moving as one without a hand to drive it. There is a small lit window in the farmhouse ahead, the same low glow that has drawn them home every evening of their lives. The path they walk was made by feet and hooves over long seasons, worn smooth by every going and every coming back. The gate is narrow, and only one may pass through at a time before the rest can follow. The field is still, and the fold is not yet closed.

For a long stretch the one who walks beside you has kept the same pace, no word between you, the ground taken step for step. There was a season when the going was easy and the pack rode light on both your shoulders, and neither of you counted the miles. The path you took together came down from those who walked it before you, worn smooth by feet you never saw, and part of the walking was learning which of that you carried and which you set down at the roadside. Nothing about this came quickly; it ripened the way a field does, one turn of the year laid over the last until the standing grain was ready to be cut. The old yew at the edge of the field drops its dark needles and stands green through the same winters that strip everything around it, and the walking that brought you here has that same slow hardiness in it. What matters now is not where the two paces first fell together, but that they held this long. The track ahead is quiet, and the fork in it waits where it has always waited.
